821: C is correct because Amazon AppFlow is a managed integration service that natively supports Salesforce as a source and Amazon Redshift as a destination, and it can run flows over an AWS PrivateLink connection so the data never traverses the public internet. Creating a PrivateLink connection in the VPC provides the private connectivity AppFlow needs with minimal setup. This combination requires the least development effort because AppFlow handles both the initial full load and ongoing incremental change capture from Salesforce. The other options either use services not designed for private Salesforce ingestion or assume network constructs that do not apply to a SaaS provider like Salesforce.
822: A is correct because Amazon S3 with the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class automatically moves objects between frequent access and infrequent access tiers based on changing access patterns, which optimizes cost for file data with unpredictable access. Since the question allows application changes, updating the application to use the S3 API for storing and retrieving files is acceptable, and S3 eliminates the cost of running EFS Standard-Infrequent Access storage for large indexed file sets. The FSx options would still require paying for provisioned file systems, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is unsuitable for files that need immediate interactive access. The index remains in RDS, so only the file storage tier changes.
823: C is correct because an Application Load Balancer operates at layer 7 and supports advanced request routing based on query strings, allowing traffic to be directed to different target groups depending on query parameter values. Attaching an ACM certificate to the ALB enables HTTPS listener encryption of the traffic in transit. This meets both the query-string routing and encryption requirements in a single managed service. Network Load Balancers operate at layer 4 and cannot inspect query strings, and Gateway Load Balancers are designed for inline virtual appliances, not web traffic routing.
824: C is correct because deploying the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer provides automatic scalability and high availability for the application tier. Amazon Aurora Serverless with MySQL compatibility provides a highly available database that automatically scales capacity based on load, replacing the single self-managed MySQL instance on EC2. Aurora also replicates data across multiple Availability Zones for fault tolerance. Redshift is not MySQL-compatible, ElastiCache is not a MySQL database, and options without Auto Scaling cannot handle increased traffic automatically.
825: B is correct because a KMS customer managed key with automatic key rotation enabled satisfies the explicit requirement that the encryption key be rotated automatically every year, since AWS KMS rotates the key material annually on the customer's behalf. Setting the S3 bucket's default encryption to use this customer managed key ensures all migrated data is encrypted at rest using that key. This approach meets the rotation requirement with essentially no ongoing operational overhead beyond the initial configuration. SSE-S3 does rotate keys but is managed entirely by AWS without a yearly rotation guarantee tied to a key the company controls, and manual rotation or imported key material adds unnecessary overhead or blocks automatic rotation.
826: B is correct because enabling AWS IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on across all AWS accounts managed in AWS Organizations. Configuring a two-way forest trust between an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory in AWS Directory Service and the company's self-managed on-premises Active Directory lets IAM Identity Center use the on-premises AD as the identity source, so users and groups continue to be managed in the existing on-premises AD. This gives centralized SSO to all member accounts without duplicating or migrating identity data. Creating a standalone AWS Directory Service directory would not preserve on-premises user management, and a trust alone without IAM Identity Center does not provide account SSO.
827: D is correct because the Aurora I/O-Optimized storage configuration eliminates charges for read and write I/O operations, charging only a slightly higher rate for storage and backup. For an application receiving large amounts of traffic with heavy database I/O, the removal of per-request I/O charges makes this the most cost-effective option as load increases. Aurora Standard and General Purpose storage continue to bill per I/O request, which becomes expensive under heavy sustained load. Provisioned IOPS is a self-managed IOPS allocation that adds cost and administrative tuning effort.
828: D is correct because AWS Security Hub is designed to aggregate and continuously monitor security posture and compliance controls across an entire organization. Designating a Security Hub delegated administrator account from the Organizations management account allows Security Hub to be enabled for all hundreds of member accounts centrally, and Security Hub supports ready-made compliance standards including NIST and PCI DSS that automatically run checks and provide proof to auditors that controls are implemented and functioning. Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability scanning service, GuardDuty is a threat detection service, and CloudTrail is an audit logging service; none of them continuously monitor control compliance against NIST and PCI DSS standards.
829: A is correct because transitioning objects to the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class is the most operationally efficient way to reduce storage costs for a data lake with unknown and changing access patterns across many teams and applications. Intelligent-Tiering automatically monitors access and moves objects between access tiers with no retrieval fees or operational intervention, while frequently accessed objects remain immediately available in the frequent access tier. Storage class analysis requires time to gather data and still requires manual lifecycle rule management, and Glacier or Lambda-based transitions either delay access or add significant operational complexity.
830: B is correct because Amazon Neptune is a fully managed graph database purpose-built for storing and querying highly connected data using vertices and edges. Many-to-many relationships like user connections are modeled natively as edges, and finding mutual connections up to five levels is a graph traversal query that Neptune executes with high performance. Relational databases and Athena require expensive recursive JOIN operations that scale poorly for multi-level relationship traversal on 10 million connections. QuickSight is a visualization tool and does not provide the needed query performance.
831: D is correct because an AWS Site-to-Site VPN can be provisioned quickly, typically within hours, using existing internet connectivity, and it is inexpensive compared to dedicated connections, which suits a low-bandwidth, small-traffic workload. AWS Direct Connect provides dedicated high bandwidth but takes weeks to provision and costs significantly more than needed here. A bastion host is not a network connectivity solution for site-to-site access, and a client VPN is designed for individual users rather than connecting an entire on-premises environment.
832: C is correct because AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed SFTP server backed by Amazon S3, and selecting AWS Directory Service as the identity provider with an AD Connector lets employees authenticate with their existing on-premises Microsoft Active Directory credentials. AD Connector proxies authentication requests to the on-premises AD without requiring any directory synchronization or replication, preserving the current authentication mechanism with minimal operational overhead. The service scales automatically and stores files in S3 for cost optimization. Running SFTP on self-managed EC2 instances or an S3 File Gateway with SMB shares does not preserve the SFTP protocol and authentication model with the least overhead.
833: C is correct because Amazon EventBridge provides a centralized event bus for the order events, and creating a separate event rule per validation step keeps each step decoupled and independently changeable. Configuring the input transformer on each rule sends only the subset of order data that the specific validation Lambda function requires, enforcing least-privilege data access. Event-driven rules also allow validation steps to be added, removed, or modified without affecting other components, satisfying the loose coupling requirement. SQS point-to-point queues with a custom transformer add coupling and management overhead, and SNS filtering cannot transform message bodies.
834: C is correct because an Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with multiple read replicas provides a writer instance for the application's create operations and dedicated reader instances for the real-time reports. Configuring the application to use the reader endpoint directs reporting queries to the read replicas, offloading that workload from the writer so new entry creation is no longer slowed by concurrent report generation. This directly addresses the previously observed performance issue while providing high availability. Using the backup instance, a single EC2 database, or refactoring to DynamoDB would not properly isolate reporting workload from writes.
835: C is correct because an S3 interface endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink allows the on-premises application to reach Amazon S3 privately over the existing Direct Connect connection without any internet access. Routing traffic from the on-premises network to the interface endpoint keeps the S3 traffic on private AWS network infrastructure. A public VIF would route traffic over AWS public endpoints, which does not align with a network designed for private access, while a NAT gateway serves outbound internet traffic from a VPC rather than on-premises traffic, and VPC peering cannot be established with an on-premises network. The interface endpoint is a cost-effective managed option that requires no internet gateway.
836: B is correct because a Route 53 multivalue answer routing policy returns multiple healthy IP addresses for the website and automatically excludes endpoints that fail health checks, so a Region where the website is unhealthy will not receive traffic. Multivalue answer supports health checks on each record and answers DNS queries with up to eight healthy records, giving both multi-Region distribution and failover behavior. A simple routing policy does not reliably route traffic away from unhealthy endpoints, and an Application Load Balancer cannot have target groups spanning instances in two different Regions.
837: C is correct because Amazon EFS is a fully managed network file system that can be mounted concurrently across many EC2 instances and spans multiple Availability Zones, providing shared access to large files without copying data between instances. Employees can continue storing and retrieving the 25 GB or larger files directly from the mounted file system on any instance, resolving the availability issues. EBS volumes can only be attached to one instance at a time, instance store volumes are ephemeral, and Amazon S3 would require transferring files rather than shared instance access, which changes the access workflow.
838: D is correct because enabling EBS encryption for the EC2 instance volumes and RDS encryption with KMS keys encrypts all data at rest, including storage, snapshots, and backups, satisfying the PII encryption mandate. These are configuration-level settings that can be enabled with minimal changes to the existing infrastructure. ACM generates TLS certificates for in-transit encryption, not storage encryption, and SSL is also a transport-layer mechanism rather than encryption at rest. CloudHSM can manage keys but requires significant infrastructure and application changes, making it unnecessary when KMS-backed service-native encryption is available.
839: C is correct because a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 is a free, highly available route-table entry that allows traffic from the Lambda function's private subnets to reach S3 directly over the AWS network without traversing the internet or the NAT instance. Updating the subnet route tables to include the gateway endpoint prefix list removes the NAT instance as a bottleneck entirely, eliminating the intermittent timeouts caused by saturated NAT traffic. Replacing or upsizing the NAT instance still routes S3 traffic through a bandwidth-constrained middleman, and a transit gateway does not provide private connectivity to S3 on its own.
840: B is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses AWS global edge locations with anycast IP addresses to receive reporter RTMP streams and accelerates TCP connections over the AWS global network backbone back to the broadcast system. This directly provides the highest quality streams and the required accelerated TCP connections for ingesters worldwide. Amazon CloudFront is a content distribution service that does not support RTMP ingest for this use case, Client VPN is a user network access tool not built for stream ingestion, and EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses provide no transport acceleration.
